I have to say, I'm impressed with the switch. I got it noon my time yesterday, then had to tortuously wait through two classes with it in my bag next to me (okay, I lied, I used one of those, a recitation, to set the thing up, and did have some time between classes to try it) before I could use it.

At launch, I had 1-2 switch and Zelda, breath of the wild. I had the grey joy cons, and bought Fast RMX as well as Snipperclips from the Eshop after I got the thing working on wifi.

The switch is an amazing device. I have never stayed up so late gaming (after I got off at 4pm my time, I played basically nonstop until 7 am, when I forced myself to sleep), and frankly, the hours melted away with it in a way they haven't since I was 8 or 9 playing shockwave games on the family generic dell brown tower of slow. This, despite the fact that I played less Breath of the wild than I did FastRMX. At an estimate (I don't believe there is a way to check total play time from the console, though last play date is there), my time breakdown, and thoughts on each title I had went as follows (spoiler free, though it does discuss the gameplay, but not the story, of Zelda breath of the wild, if you are trying to play that one completely blind, skip its section):

1.5 hours: 1-2 switch, in two sessions. One was with a 65 year old uncle, who has played exactly one other game in his life, wii sports. As he stated "I always wondered what happened to the wii." He had, of course, never heard of the switch, but kept an open mind, and was very impressed with the social aspect of the game, and the technology used; We played quickdraw and table tennis together. Asked if he would play it again, his response was "If people around me were playing it, I might, but I would not seek it out, Its cool and fun, but not something I could see myself doing instead of other things." The other portion of my 1-2 switch time was with my friends, primarily looking at it from the perspective of "we want to experience the tech in the joycon." Overall, we had a lot of fun, though the fact that you don't start with all the games unlocked was kind of annoying. After 5 or 6 games, though, you get everything.

30m: Snipperclips demo. So I knew when I saw snipperclips that I wanted it, but I did want to confirm that by downloading the demo (the only free demo in the eshop, I note). It goes through all the levels until the balloon popping one, if you have watched any footage from it. The singleplayer was disappointing, but that's not the game is. For those wondering, single player mode simply adds a button to switch between the two characters, and when you switch, the one you are no longer controlling holds their last pose and position, even if crouching or tiptoeing. I did not get any game time with a friend on Snipperclipps.

6 hours: Fast RMX: (in two sessions, each around 3 hours, broken up by a few people coming in to see the console and our playing 1-2 switch together) I was surprised by this one. After I was bored by the first hour of Zelda (I can be hard to engage with videogames. I'll kind of bounce from one game to another, accomplishing little, than find one that I just can't get away from. Zeldas slightly slow start alienated me at first). I was also unsure on purchasing the title, since my switch package came with a Redout preorder, a very similar looking game. I can say wholeheartedly that it is worth $20. It was stupidly addicting; which is not anything like my thoughts on any non mariokart racing game I've ever played before. It is fairly easy- On my first runthrough the subsonic cups, (slowest speed), I podiumed on all of them except platinum (the highest difficulty cup), though I did have to retry on two of them. I accomplished this without knowing how to play (The game lacks a tutorial at this time), and not even knowing about a very important mechanic (boosts when not on boost lanes) for the first third of the cups. That being said, I only managed to get first place once, on the easiest cup, and that was after a retry. Seeing as there are several higher speed classes, and even after 10 or so tries, I couldn't podium on platinum, the replay value here seems really good. Even though it has the F-Zero aesthetic, though, this game does NOT feel like F-zero. Controls are intentionally floaty (it felt good, actually, and added challenge), whereas Fzero is VERY precise, inputwise, and there's no story to speak of. It feels like a racing cabinet arcade game. I tried multiplayer briefly, on the switch units screen rather than my 24 inch monitor- This game benefits highly from having a large display; half of a 3 inch switch screen ain't gonna cut it, and I can't imagine 4 way split screen. I found it incredibly natural to control with one joycon held sideways.

5 hours: Zelda, Breath of the Wild: Okay, so the one you guys actually care about. I spent a few minutes on this as soon as I could, then spent a few more minutes on it at the next chance I got, then got bored and hooked myself on Fast heroin RMX. When I did decide to change back to zelda, though, I got addicted to that too. Gameplay is enticing, and they've done away with the typical zelda bullshit of not giving you most of link's classic abilities like bows and bombs until the game is about to end. Combat is well managed, though weapons break too fast, I feel, and the motion controls for aiming are too sensitive, and you CANNOT adjust sensitivity beyond a binary on/off choice. I also would have liked the ability to do things like turn up the music volume independently of sound effects and voices. Sadly, nintendo continues their tradition of telling you the best way to play their games, weather you like it or not.

BoTW does feel kind of ubisofty, though. Crafting, fast travel from the start of the game, open world map that begins hidden, dotted with towers to survey your block of wilderness, which will be dotted with enemy encampments. That being said, it has a bit of a Fallout new vegas feel to it; the game might say "Sure you can go there*" with one hell of an asterisk, the asterisk being that, if you go there, the monsters are all too hard for you, and you WILL be raped fairly quickly.

Overall, I really liked BoTW, once I got past the kind of slow start. Its shaping up to be better than windwaker, which, for me, is a VERY hard title to beat.

Thoughts on the switch unit itself.

The tablet does not feel cheap. It is REALLY small. Smaller than the adverts make it look. Its 6.4 inches, meaning that a year or two from now, smartphones will be available in the same size.

The joycons don't feel cheap, except for the buttons on the wrist strap, and the upper bumpers, which are diminutive. A warning about the wrist strap is in the list below

The switch has LOTS of little annoyances, which I've listed as follows. Most are fixable in software, though not all:

(in no particular order)

microSDcards, even those containing no gamedata, are not hotswappable.

The kickstand is flimsy as fuck, and can't really hold the unit on anything but a perfectly hard surface like a wooden table. Putting it on a carpeted floor, or even atop a cloth mousepad is a no go. Frankly, I expected this from the reveal trailer. The shot of the kickstand on the plane just oozed flimsiness.

There should be a 3.5mm audio jack on the dock. Yes, it does audio over HDMI. No, I don't want to use the crummy speakers on my monitor. The way to run speakers that aren't over HDMI is to plug them into the headphone jack after you dock the unit. A minor issue, sure, but seeing as the dock is essentially a usb 3.1c adapter to HDMI, usb, and power, I feel like this would be easy to do. Its not like there's insufficient bandwidth.

The joycon wrist straps. They feel cheap, and there's a right and a wrong way to put them on. Everyone I talked to, myself included, put them on the wrong way the first time. If you put them on the wrong way they click into place... And then jam so that you have to force them off again. The reason everyone does this is because the arrows on the joycon line up with how the joy con goes onto the console, but are the reverse of how the straps go on the joy cons. This also happens because there is actually LESS resistance to putting the strap on backwards than putting it on correctly. This is a problem that WILL lead to people breaking their stuff.

the joy con grip. It feels less awkward than expected, but still pretty bad. The worst part is, though, nintendo could have fixed all the ergonomic issues with it by moving the handlebar piece down so that it wasn't in the middle of the joycons, but instead started lower. It would then feel like a typical controller with the triggers a bit far away, instead of something that just... Doesn't form to anyones hands.

Finally, the system CANNOT output HDMI into lanscape flipped. Not an issue that will affect most users, but I keep my movie/ photo editing montior upsidedown on an arm above the rest of my displays. I keep it upside down so that the lower bezle is as thin as possible. Now, when I want to change to the switch, or from the switch to my pc output, I have to swivel that monitor 180 degrees, which is easy to do with my mount, but every time risks yanking cables out of it. I could change its orientation on my PC, of course, but nintendo should not dictate how I set up my computer.

I can answer any questions people have on the switch or any of these games, but I do have considerable work to do, so don't expect instant responses
